doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Jazz education teaches the math before the listening
summary: Vega complains that jazz education teaches patterns without immersion in recordings; Rowe agrees about codifying improvisation; Vega says academics lack real gig experience.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: remember going down to 24th Street and they had an interesting loft apartment, it was a great apartment. I remember getting up there and he had like an old school stereo system, you know a real nice sounding stereo, and he’d put that recording on of Dexter Gordon’s “Sophisticated Giant” and we just sat there, Pablo and myself I think. Pablo Carey teaches in Maine. Another one of our buds in those circles was David Glasser who plays lead alto with the Basie band. So we’d be sitting there going oh wow, and internalizing the music. Now those guys were geniuses because they understood all the harmony. So my dyslexia was just like rampant but it did not stop me from falling in love with the sound of the music, but what I’m saying is this is the issue that I have with this thing called jazz education is that we’re teaching these kids all of this math without first playing a bunch of recordings of the blues and listening, and just take that in and listen to it. Because we’re putting the cart before the horse. We’re learning all of this math but then these kids can’t play by ear. I’ll have these kids that can play triad patterns and do all of this stuff and I’ll go up to them and I’ll go [scats] and they’re going — they can’t do it. That’s a problem.

I’ve insisted that there’s a magic to improvisation, to jazz improvisation that’s not really explainable but that is a problem I think in the world of education because you can’t teach a four year program on jazz without getting into the codifying of it. I mean how are you going to adjust —

How do you apply it? Well codifying, how do you explain it all, and how do you put it into words? The problem here I would say is that many of the academics that are coming out here right now understand the math of it but they’ve never put a set list together in Europe trying to figure out who — well the heck with Europe, I’ve done that enough times, I’m talking about they haven’t even done a local gig looking into the audience and going okay we’ve got to play this, let’s try this, let’s read the audience. Instead they’ve got to go in there and just going to play their stuff, and play all the patterns and everything that they learned, but there’s a major disconnect, there’s a huge disconnect. All right but what we have to talk about here is that there are a lot of major jazz artists that play by ear. Stan Getz.
